chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from al-Saffan, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about a man who made it a vow upon himself to walk to the House of God, but he was unable to do so; he said: 'He performs Hajj riding.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: 'There is no contradiction between these narrations, because that which is obligatory upon one who vows to walk to the Sacred House of God is to fulfill it if he is able to do so and has the capacity, to the extent that he should stand on his feet in the passage.'
If he is unable to do so and cannot walk, it is permissible for him to ride, provided that he drives along with him a camel or a cow.
If he is unable to do that [drive an animal], then let him ride and there is no penalty upon him.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for someone who vows to walk to Mecca for Hajj but cannot?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar clarifies the juristic principle of 'ease in hardship' (al-yusr) regarding vow fulfillment, with Imam al-Hasan resolving apparent contradictions by emphasizing that the vow's core obligation is to perform Hajj, not the specific mode of transport. The ruling establishes a graduated flexibility: while walking is preferred, riding is permissible if walking is impossible, with the additional requirement of driving a sacrificial animal only if one has the means to do so. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on proportional obligation based on individual capacity.
